metadata.title: Reproduction Package for SEFM 2026 Submission `Revisiting Sequentialization of Concurrent C Programs'
metadata.description:
Reproduction Package for the Paper “Revisiting Sequentialization of Concurrent C Programs”

Abstract

This artifact is a reproduction package for the paper “Revisiting Sequentialization of Concurrent C Programs” submitted for SEFM 2026 (https://sefm-conference.github.io/2026/).

This paper presents CPAmpor, a highly configurable sequentialization tool for concurrent C programs implemented in the actively maintained tool CPAchecker. CPAmpor is compatible with many sequential backends and provides novel encodings of partial order reduction strategies directly within the sequentialized program.

This artifact consists of all executables, input data and results required to reproduce the experiments. In particular, it also contains the original results of the paper and a way to generate the HTML and CSV files used for the papers tables and plots.

A full reproduction of the experiments requires roughly 200 days of CPU time. However, the benchmarks are configurable and parallelizable to reduce the amount of elapsed time. The experiments for each RQ can be run in isolation, and we provide shorter configurations for each RQ that run a representative subset of the tasks in less than 1 hour each. To test that everything is working as intended, we provide a Smoketest that takes roughly 20 minutes.

Claimed Badges

We claim the following badges in this artifact:

  • Available: The artifact is available on Zenodo
  • Functional and Reusable: There are explanations in this README to run the experiments and add a new tool to the experimental setup.

0. Table of Contents

This README contains the following sections to help users reproduce the experiments:

  • TL;DR: A quick guide to reproduce the experiments and analyze the data.
  • Directory Structure: An overview of directories (and their purpose) that are part of this artifact.
  • Requirements: Describes the software + hardware requirements for the artifact to work properly.
  • Running Experiments Describes how to execute, configure and parallelize the experiments, including a quick Smoketest.
  • Interpreting Results: Describes where the experiment results can be found and how to analyze them.
  • Information for Reuse: Documentation on how to use the artifact for purposes other than reproduction.
  • Used Versions: An overview of all benchmark and tool versions in this artifact.
  • Known Issues: Describes known issues when executing the artifact and how to mitigate them.

1. TL;DR

Note: All commands in this README should be executed from the root directory, i.e., the directory that contains this README.

  • Start up the CAV 2026 VM (available at https://zenodo.org/records/19184839) using, e.g., VirtualBox.
  • Download and extract the artifacts ZIP file into the VM, ideally not in a shared folder but in a VM local folder.
  • Run the following to setup the VM correctly. The script will ask once for the admin password which is cav for the CAV 2026 VM. The VM will reboot after everything is finished.
bash setup_vm.sh              # takes 3 minutes
  • After rebooting, run one or more of the following commands to run the experiments and obtain the results. All times refer to CPU time.
make run_artifact_smoketest   # takes 20 minutes
make run_artifact_rq1_short   # takes 1 hour
make run_artifact_rq2_short   # takes 1 hour
make run_artifact_rq3_short   # takes 1 hour
make run_artifact_rq4_short   # takes 1 hour
make run_artifact_full        # takes 200 days
make run_artifact_rq1         # takes 3 days
make run_artifact_rq2         # takes 45 days
make run_artifact_rq3         # takes 75 days
make run_artifact_rq4         # takes 80 days
  • The file doc/smoketest-output.txt contains the expected output on the terminal when running the Smoketest.
  • The results of the experiments can be obtained in the results dir (or results-smoketest for the Smoketest or results-short for the short experiments). This directory will be generated when running the corresponding experiments and is not provided in the artifact. Each RQ has its own subdirectory results/rq{1, 2, 3, 4}/.
  • The subdirectories results/rq{1, 2, 3, 4}/*.results.table/ contain summary statistics for the experiments in HTML files that were used for the tables in our paper. The numbers reported in these HTML files should match the numbers of the HTML files in results-paper/rq{1, 2, 3, 4}/. Note that this only holds for the full experiments, since the Smoketest and the short experiments execute a subset of the programs only.
  • rq{1, 3, 4} contain subdirectories named plot with PDF plot files that should match the figures in our paper.

2. Directory Structure

This artifact contains the following items:

  • README.md: This file.
  • benchmarks: Contains (i) BenchExec, (ii) the subset of SV-Benchmarks used in the evaluation, and (iii) the XML files define benchmarks (used tool, timelimit, used tasks, etc.) that can be given to BenchExec for execution. The .set files list the programs to sequentialize: sv-benchmarks/c/Concurrency.set for the full experiments, sv-benchmarks-short/Concurrency-rq{1, 2, 3, 4}-short.set for the short experiments, and sv-benchmarks-smoketest/Concurrency-smoketest.set for the Smoketest.
  • doc: Contains documentation on expected output on the terminal.
  • results (Will be generated when running the full experiments): After running the full experiments, the results dir appears and contains summary HTML tables and CSV files (both produced by BenchExec) and logfiles (produced by the respective tools).
  • results-short (Will be generated when running the short experiments): Same as results, but when executing the short instead of the full experiments.
  • results-smoketest (Will be generated when running the smoketest): Same as results, but when executing the Smoketest instead of the full experiments.
  • results-paper: Contains the original result files (HTML, CSV, logfiles) from our evaluation. The numbers match exactly the ones reported in our paper and will not be changed by any of the commands presented in this README.
  • scripts/python: Contains several Python scripts that automate the artifact, such as task extraction or wrapper scripts for CPAmpor and Lazy-CSeq.
  • sequentializations: After running CPAmpor and Lazy-CSeq, this directory contains the sequentialized C programs and the YML task definitions with expected verdicts for properties (data races, reachability, memory safety, overflows).
  • tools: Contains (i) CPAmpor and Lazy-CSeq that create the sequentialized programs and (ii) the backends 2ls, Bubaak, CBMC, CPAchecker, Mopsa, Symbiotic, and Ultimate Kojak that analyze the programs produced by CPAmpor and Lazy-CSeq.

Note that there are several subdirectories suffixed with -modified; these contain small adjustments to files in some of the used tools. Each of these directories contains a separate README explaining what changes were made and why they were made. The changes are all necessary for the artifact to work properly.

3. Requirements

All tools in this artifact were compiled for a x86 architecture, so it will in general not be possible to run them on an ARM chip.

The unpacked artifact needs 2GB of disk space, and for the VM image we recommend at least 16 GB of additional disk space.

The artifact requires a VM with at least 4 cores and 20 GB of memory to run it properly. The Smoketest can be executed with 2 cores and 8 GB of memory.

We tested this artifact with the VM used for artifacts submitted to the CAV 2026 conference (https://zenodo.org/records/19184839). The artifact was tested with version VirtualBox VM 7.2.12 r174389 linux.amd64. Any other VM will likely also work with this artifact if set up correctly, but the CAV 2026 VM has several requirements pre-installed already.

For all further requirements, please take a look at setup_vm.sh, which installs all required dependencies into the VM and sets up the environment correctly.

4. Experiments

4.1. Setup

All data and tools are contained inside the artifacts ZIP file already. Only the CAV 2026 VM and some small dependencies and system changes are required for the artifact to run.

From the root folder of the extracted files, run the following to set up the VM correctly:

bash setup_vm.sh

The script will ask once for the sudo password which is cav for the CAV 2026 VM. The setup installs some dependencies used by BenchExec and some of the backends that are not pre-installed in the CAV 2026 VM. In addition, the system is configured so that BenchExec can execute without issue, such as user privileges, cgroups, and systemd. The script may take several minutes to complete and will reboot the VM after everything is finished.

4.2. Benchmark Selection

Depending on your available resources you can select different sets of benchmarks to execute the tools on. You have the following options:

  • A smoke test with 2 programs which can be useful to test that the artifact is behaving as intended:
make run_artifact_smoketest   # takes 20 minutes
  • Shorter benchmarks for each RQ, that execute a representative subset of the programs (see Short Benchmarks):
make run_artifact_rq1_short   # takes 1 hour
make run_artifact_rq2_short   # takes 1 hour
make run_artifact_rq3_short   # takes 1 hour
make run_artifact_rq4_short   # takes 1 hour
  • The full benchmark set used in the experiments for the paper:
make run_artifact_full        # takes 200 days
  • Each RQ can be run in isolation using the following:
make run_artifact_rq1         # takes 3 days
make run_artifact_rq2         # takes 45 days
make run_artifact_rq3         # takes 75 days
make run_artifact_rq4         # takes 80 days

4.3. Benchmark Configuration and Parallelization

The root Makefile exposes some of BenchExecs CLI so that time, memory and CPU limits that are specified in XML files can be overridden. This can be useful to reduce the elapsed time it takes for the benchmark to run. Each of the following commands are used for a single tool invocation on a single program, except for NUM_OF_THREADS as described below.

  • LIMIT_CORES=C (default 4) sets the amount C of CPU cores.
  • TIMELIMIT=S (default 900) sets the timelimit S in seconds.
  • MEMORYLIMIT=M (default 15000) sets the memory limit M in MB.
  • NUM_OF_THREADS=T (default 1) sets the amount of parallel runs to execute. For example, 1 corresponds to a sequential execution, but 2 will invoke a tool twice on different programs in parallel.

Note that the Smoketest is not affected by these settings since it uses much smaller default values and terminates quickly anyway. If you still wish to adjust the Smoketest, adjust the values in the Makefile accordingly. The short benchmarks set their own TIMELIMIT (900s, except 100s for RQ2) which cannot be overridden on the command line either, but all other settings above (e.g. NUM_OF_THREADS) still apply to them.

4.3.1. Parallelization Example

Assume you set up the VM with 40 GB of memory and 8 CPU cores, then 2 tool invocations can be run in parallel:

make run_artifact_full LIMIT_CORES=4 TIMELIMIT=900 MEMORYLIMIT=15000 NUM_OF_THREADS=2

Or, if you wish to increase the parallelism further, you can reduce LIMIT_CORES. The MEMORYLIMIT however needs to be adjusted too in this case since there can be 4 runs in parallel, but the machine only has 40 GB so it cannot perform 4 runs with 15 GB of memory safely.

make run_artifact_full LIMIT_CORES=2 TIMELIMIT=900 MEMORYLIMIT=7500 NUM_OF_THREADS=4

Note that TIMELIMIT=900 is relatively high since the vast majority of tasks are solved in 100 seconds or less, and most of the CPU time is spent on the programs that timeout, i.e., that take the full 900 seconds. Therefore you could reduce the TIMELIMIT and check whether the amount of solved tasks within a given time is roughly equal to the values observed in the original plots in the paper:

make run_artifact_full LIMIT_CORES=4 TIMELIMIT=300 MEMORYLIMIT=15000 NUM_OF_THREADS=2

If possible, we recommend to run the full experiments with the highest possible value for NUM_OF_THREADS (based on the available hardware), and all other commands left at their default. Otherwise, the benchmarks will not be under the same conditions as the benchmarks conducted for the paper and you may observe significant differences in the results.

4.4. Smoketest

The Smoketest creates sequentializations by CPAmpor and Lazy-CSeq for 2 simple programs in different configurations and gives it to all necessary backends which ensures that:

  • the sequentialization process works for both CPAmpor and Lazy-CSeq
  • the benchmark files are present and can be read by CPAmpor and Lazy-CSeq
  • the backend verifiers can be run without issue
  • BenchExec actually produces results that can be retrieved
  • the plot script works as intended

The file doc/smoketest-output.txt contains the expected output on the terminal when running the Smoketest.

4.5. Short Benchmarks

The short benchmarks execute exactly the same Run Sets (i.e., tools, configurations, and properties) as the full experiments of an RQ, but only on a subset of the programs, so that each RQ takes less than 1 hour of CPU time instead of several days:

make run_artifact_rq1_short   # takes 1 hour
make run_artifact_rq2_short   # takes 1 hour
make run_artifact_rq3_short   # takes 1 hour
make run_artifact_rq4_short   # takes 1 hour

The subsets are defined in the following files, which list programs of benchmarks/sv-benchmarks/c/ just like the full task set Concurrency.set (the files are also copied into benchmarks/sv-benchmarks/c/, where they are read from):

Task Set File Programs Timelimit
benchmarks/sv-benchmarks-short/Concurrency-rq1-short.set 76 900s
benchmarks/sv-benchmarks-short/Concurrency-rq2-short.set 9 100s
benchmarks/sv-benchmarks-short/Concurrency-rq3-short.set 13 900s
benchmarks/sv-benchmarks-short/Concurrency-rq4-short.set 13 900s

The programs were selected using the original results in results-paper/: for every program we summed up the CPU time of all runs of an RQ that use this program, and then picked programs such that the total stays below 1 hour (roughly 45 min on the hardware used for the paper) while covering as many program families (pthread, pthread-wmm, weaver, …), both expected verdicts, and all three properties (Reach Safety, Memory Safety, Overflows) as the budget allows. Only programs that all configurations of an RQ sequentialize successfully were considered, so that all Run Sets of an RQ contain the same programs. Note that the number of programs differs per RQ because the number of runs per program does: RQ1 executes up to 6 Run Sets on each program, whereas RQ2 executes up to 30 (6 Run Sets for each of the 5 backends) and RQ3 and RQ4 execute up to 36 each (a program is only executed in the Run Sets of the properties it defines).

Since the selection favors programs that are solved quickly, the short benchmarks keep the timelimit of 900s that was used for the paper (except for RQ2, where 5 backends are executed and a timelimit of 900s would allow for a handful of programs only). The absolute numbers reported by the short benchmarks are therefore much smaller than the numbers in the paper, but the results for the selected programs should match the corresponding rows of the HTML tables in results-paper/.

5. Interpreting Results

The results of the full experiments can be found in the results directory that is created in the root directory. For the Smoketest and the short benchmarks, the directory is named results-smoketest or results-short but they behave exactly like results so we refer only to results in this section.

results should contain four directories rq{1, 2, 3, 4} with files generated by BenchExec and by our plot script. The directories rq{1, 3, 4} contain a subdirectory named plot that contains the PDF files used to visualize the results. Note that for rq2 there is no plot directory, since the paper had no plots for RQ2.

5.1. HTML Tables

BenchExec generates HTML files with summaries and details for benchmark runs. After the experiments finished, the HTML files can be found in results/rq.../rq...results.table/, i.e., every directory containing the HTML files is suffixed with results.table.

A simple HTML file example can be found in the directory results-paper/rq1/cbmc/. The main page of the HTML files contains the analysis backend, the used versions, the benchmark limits (timelimit, memory, CPU cores), the OS, and the used hardware, and Summary Statistics at the bottom.

The Summary Statistics contain the amount of correct (split into true / false) and incorrect (split into true / false) results for each Run Set. We used the numbers from the Summary Statistics in the tables of our paper.

5.1.1. Comparing Artifact and Paper Results

To compare if the full experiments of the artifact produces results that match the experiment results from the paper, you can compare the Summary Statistics of two HTML tables. The Artifact HTML File should match the Paper HTML File, which can be found in the following directories:

Artifact HTML Directory Paper HTML Directory
results/rq1/rq1-cbmc.results.table/ results-paper/rq1/cbmc/
   
results/rq2/rq2-2ls.results.table/ results-paper/rq2/2ls/
results/rq2/rq2-bubaak.results.table/ results-paper/rq2/bubaak/
results/rq2/rq2-mopsa.results.table/ results-paper/rq2/mopsa/
results/rq2/rq2-symbiotic.results.table/ results-paper/rq2/symbiotic/
results/rq2/rq2-ultimatekojak.results.table/ results-paper/rq2/ultimatekojak/
   
results/rq3/rq3-cbmc.results.table/ results-paper/rq3/cbmc/
results/rq3/rq3-cpachecker.results.table/ results-paper/rq3/cpachecker/
   
results/rq4/rq4-cbmc.results.table/ results-paper/rq4/cbmc/
results/rq4/rq4-cpachecker.results.table/ results-paper/rq4/cpachecker/

The Run Sets contain a unique name that can be used to link them to specific tables in the paper. The file results-paper/README.md contains a full list of all Run Set names and how they link to the numbers presented in the tables of the paper.

5.1.2. Differences to Paper Numbers

Some Run Sets may contain noticeable differences to the numbers reported in our paper. This can of course be due to a different environment (OS, Hardware, …), but also due to tools that are not consistent across runs. We observed relatively stable result numbers (up to +-3) across runs for all backends except for the Overflows analysis of CPAchecker where the difference in correct results can be up to +-10 (from ~360 correct results).

5.2. CSV Plots

The plot directories contain PDF files that are created from the CSV data obtained from BenchExec. Note that the plots in the paper were created from LaTeX, so the PDF plots will differ visually even though they are configured to match the plots in the paper.

6. Information for Reuse

6.1. Running CPAmpor on a Single File

Since CPAchecker, which includes CPAmpor, is compiled to a binary in this artifact already, this artifact is a good place to try out our sequentialization.

Simply run:

./tools/cpachecker/bin/cpachecker --sequentializeProgram \
  ./benchmarks/sv-benchmarks/c/pthread/lazy01.i

The output indicates that the program can be found in ./output/sequentializedProgram.c relative to where the command is run, in this case from the root directory:

Sequentialized program exported to:  ./output/sequentializedProgram.c

6.1.1. CPAmpor Configuration

If you wish to configure the sequentialization, take a look at the options for CPAmpor at tools/cpachecker/doc/ConfigurationOptions.txt. Starting in line 309, the options for CPAmpor are described in detail.

For example, enable EUC partial order reduction with a DENSE encoding (in this case HEXADECIMAL) and ACCESS precision:

./tools/cpachecker/bin/cpachecker --sequentializeProgram \
  ./benchmarks/sv-benchmarks/c/pthread/lazy01.i \
  --option analysis.algorithm.MPOR.bitVectorEncoding=HEXADECIMAL \
  --option analysis.algorithm.MPOR.partialOrderReductionMode=ACCESS_ONLY \
  --option analysis.algorithm.MPOR.executeThreadsUntilConflict=true

6.1.2. Prevent Overwriting

By default, the sequentialization is exported to ./output/sequentializedProgram.c. So if you invoke CPAmpor twice, then the program is overwritten. If you wish to prevent overwriting you can specify the output file name relative to ./output/:

./tools/cpachecker/bin/cpachecker --sequentializeProgram \
  ./benchmarks/sv-benchmarks/c/pthread/lazy01.i \
  --option analysis.preprocessing.MPOR.programPath="lazy01-sequentialized.c"

6.2. Adding a new Analysis Backend

If you wish to add another analysis backend, first make sure that a Python file exists in the directory benchmarks/benchexec/benchexec/tools/. This ensures that BenchExec is compatible with the new backend, e.g., that it can parse the tools output and report the results correctly.

Let us choose Ultimate Automizer as the new backend and evaluate it on the tasks for RQ2. First the new backend needs to be downloaded and placed into the tools directory. You can do this by adding a new target to tools/Makefile:

download_ultimateautomizer:
    rm -rf ultimateautomizer && mkdir -p ultimateautomizer
    wget https://zenodo.org/records/17749227/files/uautomizer.zip -O uautomizer.zip
    unzip uautomizer.zip -d ultimateautomizer
    rm uautomizer.zip
    mv ultimateautomizer/UAutomizer-linux/* ultimateautomizer/
    rmdir ultimateautomizer/UAutomizer-linux

In this case Ultimate Automizer contains a wrapper directory UAutomizer-linux that we remove so that BenchExec can find the executable of Ultimate Automizer inside the directory tools/ultimateautomizer/. This may not be necessary for all backends, for example the target download_symbiotic contains no such wrapper directory and can be extracted directly.

Then, a new target needs to be created in the root Makefile:

run_artifact_ultimateautomizer:
    cd ./sequentializations/ && make copy_property_files
    cd ./sequentializations/ && make sequentialize_rq2      # could also be sequentialize_rq{1, 3, 4}
    cd ./benchmarks/ && make run_benchexec_ultimateautomizer \
        LIMIT_CORES=$(LIMIT_CORES) TIMELIMIT=$(TIMELIMIT) \
        MEMORYLIMIT=$(MEMORYLIMIT) NUM_OF_THREADS=$(NUM_OF_THREADS)
    @echo "ultimateautomizer benchmark finished successfully."

Next we need to ensure that the target run_benchexec_ultimateautomizer exists in benchmarks/Makefile, so add the following there:

run_benchexec_ultimateautomizer:
    rm -rf $(RESULTS_PATH_FROM_MAKEFILE)ultimateautomizer/
    mkdir -p $(RESULTS_PATH_FROM_MAKEFILE)ultimateautomizer/

    cd ../tools/ultimateautomizer/ \
        && $(BENCHEXEC_PATH) $(XML_PATH)ultimateautomizer.xml     --tool-directory . \
            -o $(RESULTS_PATH_FROM_TOOL)ultimateautomizer/   --limitCores $(LIMIT_CORES) \
            --timelimit $(TIMELIMIT)s --memorylimit "$(MEMORYLIMIT) MB"  \
            --numOfThreads $(NUM_OF_THREADS) --read-only-dir / --overlay-dir /home \
        && $(TABLE_GENERATOR_PATH) \
            $(RESULTS_PATH_FROM_TOOL)ultimateautomizer/ultimateautomizer.*.xml.bz2 \
            -o $(RESULTS_PATH_FROM_TOOL)ultimateautomizer/ultimateautomizer$(TABLE_DIR_SUFFIX)/

Lastly, the XML file needs to be created for BenchExec. The easiest way to do this is to copy and modify an existing XML file. In this case we copy the XML file that contains the Run Sets for RQ2 executed by Ultimate Kojak, and replace the specified tool. Note that this will only work if sequentialize_rq2 was executed, otherwise BenchExec will report an error because there are no tasks to execute. If any other RQ was sequentialized, then ideally define a different XML file to copy from such as ./benchmarks/xml-definitions/rq1-cbmc.xml and then adjust the specified tool accordingly.

cp ./benchmarks/xml-definitions/rq2-ultimatekojak.xml ./benchmarks/xml-definitions/ultimateautomizer.xml
sed -i 's/ultimatekojak/ultimateautomizer/g' ./benchmarks/xml-definitions/ultimateautomizer.xml
sed -i 's/UKojak/UAutomizer/g' ./benchmarks/xml-definitions/ultimateautomizer.xml

Since Ultimate Kojak and Ultimate Automizer share the same CLI commands, the XML file can be reused. If you wish to add a tool other than Ultimate Automizer, then the CLI commands specified inside the XML file may need to be adjusted. Example:

<!-- this command is specific to Ultimate Kojak and Ultimate Automizer --> 
<option name="--full-output" />
<!-- replace with any number of CLI commands in the following format: --> 
<option name="*command-line argument for tool*">*optional value for command-line argument*</option>

Now that we have extended this artifact with a new tool, we can start benchmarking by running the following from the root directory:

cd ./tools && make download_ultimateautomizer
cd .. && make run_artifact_ultimateautomizer

Now the directory results/ultimateautomizer/ultimateautomizer.results.table/ should contain an HTML file. In case there are unexpected errors, e.g. due to missing dependencies for the new tool, take a look at the ZIP logfiles in results/ultimateautomizer/.

7. Used Versions

The benchmark and tool versions used in this artifact and in the paper are as follows.

Benchmarking:

  • BenchExec: https://github.com/sosy-lab/benchexec/releases/tag/3.34
  • SV-Benchmarks: https://gitlab.com/sosy-lab/benchmarking/sv-benchmarks/-/commit/6f75c45a593d3c5af05bf8732335c7cf67cee4ef

Sequentializations:

  • CPAmpor (same as CPAchecker): https://gitlab.com/sosy-lab/software/cpachecker/-/commit/f27088fd83c037615da8f463fd75046538bcfe7f
  • Lazy-CSeq: https://zenodo.org/records/17722257.

Backends:

  • 2ls: https://zenodo.org/records/10184626
  • Bubaak: https://zenodo.org/records/14205712
  • CBMC: https://github.com/diffblue/cbmc/releases/tag/cbmc-6.9.0
  • CPAchecker (same as CPAmpor): https://gitlab.com/sosy-lab/software/cpachecker/-/commit/f27088fd83c037615da8f463fd75046538bcfe7f
  • Mopsa: https://zenodo.org/records/17696794
  • Symbiotic: https://zenodo.org/records/17698724
  • Ultimate Kojak: https://zenodo.org/records/17735263

8. Known Issues

8.1. BenchExec PermissionError for cbmc.py

If BenchExec reports a PermissionError on cbmc.py, then it cannot execute cbmc.py due to a user and/or group mismatch. This can occur, for example, if the ZIP file of this artifact is extracted into a VirtualBox Shared Folder that is shared between the file systems of your actual machine and the VM. Then cbmc.py is linked to nouser and nogroup and cannot be executed. This issue can be prevented by moving the artifact ZIP file out of the VirtualBox Shared Folder into a VM local folder, and then extracting the files.

metadata.title: Data for Large parameter uncertainty persists in soil food web models integrating stoichiometry, respiration and assimilation
metadata.description:
Data and Code Description

This repository contains the data and model code used to replicate the results of a recently accepted paper examining parameter and structural uncertainty in soil food web models.

Data

  • The data includes:
    • Macrofauna data
    • Resource base information
    • Selected model parameters
  • To fully replicate the analysis, you will also need:
    • The StoicLife database DOI: 10.1038/s41597-025-04852-w
    • Data from the cited papers by Lang et al. DOI: 10.1111/oik.04419
    • Feeding guide data from Potapov et al. DOI: 10.1111/brv.12832

However, if you only wish to reproduce the model results without sourcing the original datasets, you can use the provided .RDS files (feedingmats_Itatinga and properties_Itatinga). These files allow you to run scripts 2–4 without rebuilding communities or downloading additional data.

Code

  • The scripts include all code for the model analysis. Scripts are numbered in sequence, with letters indicating subroutines or related analyses.

Script Overview:

  1. Script 1: Loads data and builds communities for model input.
  2. Script 2: Performs food web analysis, including parameter draws and data summarization.
  3. Script 3: Conducts parameter sensitivity analysis by systematically modifying each parameter.
  4. Script 4: Runs the 13C tracer experiment.
  5. Script 5: Supplemental question about Coleoptera feeding.
  6. Script 6: Supplemental question about adding mesofauna.

metadata.title: D6.3 - DMP - Data Management Plan
metadata.description:
Deliverable 6.3 comprises a comprehensive Data Management Plan (DMP), which outlines the specifics of the data that will be collected and/or generated through the entire span of the project. As it deals with all data deriving from every activity that will be performed in the context of the project, the role of the DMP is transversal to all Work Packages (WP).

Besides outlining the type, format, size, source, and purpose/utility of the data, along with its associated metadata, it also details strategies for achieving findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability of information. Furthermore, it defines policies concerning data security, preservation, and ethical and legal considerations related to data sharing and assigns responsibilities to the Data Manager.

The DMP is a living document that will undergo periodic reviews at yearly intervals during the project, specifically at months 18 and 30. These reviews will ensure that the DMP remains fit for purpose both during and after the project, especially as new data accumulate.

The DUT Partnership wish to promote open, transparent and robust urban and global change research by encouraging more open sharing of research data, leading to wider data analysis, more data re-use, and the combination of datasets from multiple sources. The DUT Partnership believe that an increased emphasis on the open sharing of research data has the potential to stimulate new approaches to the collection, analysis, validation and management of data, and to the transparency of the research process.

The DUT Partnership also recognise that not all research data can be shared openly, and that there will be legitimate reasons to constrain access, for example the risks to the privacy of individuals must always be considered where data arise from, or are derived from, personally identifiable data.

metadata.title: Royal statue of King Béhanzin
metadata.description: This sculpture is attributed to Sossa Dede, a sculptor coming from Abomey, kingdom of Danhomè (today Benin). The sculpture represents the King Béhanzin in a shark shaped armour. The peculiar shape of his armour refers to the wish of the King Béhanzin to fight against the French population.

metadata.title: Report of the first Indigenous and local knowledge dialogue workshop for the IPBES second global assessment
metadata.description:
This report summarizes the proceedings from the first Indigenous and local knowledge (ILK) dialogue workshop for the second global assessment of biodiversity and ecosystem services that is being developed by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystems Services (IPBES).

The dialogue workshop was held in Windsor, Canada from 3 to 7 November 2025. It aimed to provide a platform for discussion between Indigenous Peoples and local communities and authors of the second global assessment, with a focus on key ILK concepts, themes, questions, challenges, opportunities, resources and other issues relating to the assessment.

The workshop also discussed methods for working with ILK in IPBES assessments, which contributes to ongoing efforts to review and enhance the ways that IPBES engages with ILK. That aspect of the workshop will be covered in a separate report. 

This report aims to provide a written record of the parts of the dialogue workshop relevant to the second global assessment. It is intended to serve as a reference for assessment authors as they develop the assessment, as well as for dialogue participants and others interested in biodiversity and ILK, who may wish to review and contribute to this work in the future. 

The report does not aim to provide a comprehensive account or to resolve all the thought provoking discussions that took place. Instead, it offers a written record of those discussions, which are expected to continue to develop and evolve in the months and years. For this reason, the report highlights both areas of agreement and instances where participants expressed differing perspectives, to encourage further reflection and dialogue.

metadata.title: Report of the first Indigenous and local knowledge dialogue workshop for the IPBES business and biodiversity assessment
metadata.description:
This is the report of the first Indigenous and local knowledge (ILK) dialogue workshop for the methodological assessment of the impact and dependence of business on biodiversity and nature’s contributions to people (the “business and biodiversity assessment”), which is being developed by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystems Services (IPBES).

The workshop was held in Bogota from 23 to 24 September 2023. The dialogue workshop aimed to provide a platform for discussion between Indigenous Peoples and local communities (IPLCs) and assessment authors, with a focus on key ILK concepts, themes, questions, challenges, opportunities, resources and other issues relating to the business and biodiversity assessment.

This report aims to provide a written record of the dialogue workshop, which can be used by assessment authors to inform their work on the assessment, and by all dialogue participants who may wish to review and contribute to the work of the assessment moving forward, as well as others who may be interested in subjects relating to business, biodiversity and IPLCs.

The report is not intended to be comprehensive or give final resolution to the many interesting discussions and debates that took place during the workshop. Instead, it is intended as a written record of the discussions, and this conversation will continue to evolve over the coming months and years. For this reason, clear points of agreement are discussed, but also, if there were diverging views among participants, these are also presented for further attention and discussion.

metadata.title: Animals for Sarcophagus Decoration - Monkey 2
metadata.description: How were monkey mummies created in ancient Egypt? What significance did they have? What kind of process led to the creation of the vast monkey cemeteries that archaeologists have discovered among Egyptian ruins? As with most historical questions, the answers are complex.  The monkeys discovered inside these mummy wrappings were the ancestors of today's Egyptian Mau monkeys. Some are clearly identifiable as one of the two wildmonkey sub-species thought to have interbred to eventually produce Egypt's domestic monkeys: the jungle monkey, Felis chaus, and the African wild monkey, Felis silvestris libyca.  What is a votive gift? We don't see them much in Western Christianity today. The candles bought and lit alongside the altars in some churches are as close as most of us ever come to this ancient practice. The word "votive" here refers to something given or dedimonkeyed as an expression of a wish or desire. In Roman Egypt (which is when ACOOE takes place) the people believed that if they bought a mummified monkey and presented it to the temple of a goddess like Bast/Bastet, or Pakhet, the monkey's spirit would join the goddess in the afterlife, where it would continually urge her to bless the giver and answer their prayer, whatever it might be. Of course millions of other animal mummies were given in the same way to their respective gods–snakes, fish, mice, gazelles, ibis, crocodiles, sheep, monkeytle, falcons, dogs, and even beetles.

metadata.title: Lion of Mosul at The Mosul Museum, Iraq
metadata.description: From Nimrud (ancient Kalhu), northern IraqNeo-Assyrian, about 883-859 BC     In 2014 the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL) occupied the Mosul Museum in Iraq as it was about to reopen after years of rebuilding. The group claimed that its statues were against Islam and threatened to destroy the museum's contents. On 26th February 2015, a day after burning books from Mosul libraries, the group released a video showing the destruction of the artifacts in the museum.  To rise against the rhetoric of hate with which these acts of destruction have been associated and instead focusing on a message of hope, numerous communites from across the world united to create a means of protecting and restoring these lost cultural relics. This group of likeminded people formed Project Mosul, a volunteer initiative intending to create virtual models of the objects. The group aim to preserve our shared memory and connections to our cultural heritage, even renew and invigorate it, regardless of the acts of destruction currently being perpetrated upon it (source).  The project uses crowd-sourced images, calling out to past visitors of the museums to submit their photographs in order to virtually recreate the artefacts in 3D using the latest in photogrammetry techniques. The 3D representations are now presented in an online museum where the data is freely accessible to the public. Using the internet as a non-political, free ground for making these works available to anyone around the world.  The 3D objects may initially serve in helping identify stolen items and aid researchers working on the destroyed items. Virtual reconstruction is not an end in itself, however, but the start of a reengagement with the meaning of these objects. It is hoped that the virtual representations will give an additional tool to the communities that wish to think about, learn about, and work on the preservation and dissemination of these important elements of a national, regional and global history, and to return a sense of agency to those left helpless in the face of the destruction of their heritage.  With a team proficient in 3D designer, academic art historians and photogrammetry researchers, Scan The World is aiming to help the project expand further. Through displacing the textures from the images provided, the team aims to recreate the artifacts as fully 3D printable pieces, as photographically accurate as possible. The texture of the 3D models mask much of the quality of the sculpture which is why a lot of time is taken to ensure that the models we produce for Project Mosul and the rest of the Scan The World archive are as true to the original referent as possible.  These revived sculptures will be made physically available to anyone and aim to accurately restore the pieces to their rightful glory.     Archival information  This gigantic standing lion, roaring angrily, formed one of a pair carved half in the round which once flanked the entrance of a small temple dedicated to the goddess Ishtar, adjoining the palace of King Ashurnasirpal II (reigned 883-859 BC). The temple was excavated by Henry Layard in 1849.  The placing of figures of lions beside the doors of temples or the gates of cities was an ancient custom in Mesopotamia. Actual lions were common in the region and survived there until the nineteenth century.  The fifth leg is an artistic convention to enable the figure to be seen either from the side, walking, or from the front, standing. Compare this with the colossal statue of a winged human-headed bull from the palace of Ashurnasirpal II, also in the British Museum.     The lion is covered with a dedication in cuneiform, consisting of a prayer by Ashurnasirpal to a version of Ishtar called Sharrat-niphi, followed by a record of some of his achievements. Ishtar was one of the most important deities of Assyria. Here main cult centres were at Nineveh and Arbela. The lioness was her symbol as the goddess of fertility and warfare.

metadata.title: Aurora
metadata.description: In Roman mythology, Aurora renews herself every morning and flies across the sky, announcing the arrival of the sun. Her parentage was flexible: for Ovid, she could equally be Pallantis, signifying the daughter of Pallas, or the daughter of Hyperion. She has two siblings, a brother (Sol, the sun) and a sister (Luna, the moon). Rarely Roman writers imitated Hesiod and later Greek poets and named Aurora as the mother of the Anemoi (the Winds), who were the offspring of Astraeus, the father of the stars.  Aurora appears most often in sexual poetry with one of her mortal lovers. A myth taken from the Greek by Roman poets tells that one of her lovers was the prince of Troy, Tithonus. Tithonus was a mortal, and would therefore age and die. Wanting to be with her lover for all eternity, Aurora asked Jupiter to grant immortality to Tithonus. Jupiter granted her wish, but she failed to ask for eternal youth to accompany his immortality, and he became forever old. Aurora turned him into a cicada.

metadata.title: Seated Amida, the Buddha of the Western Paradise at the Sainsbury Centre for Visual Arts, Norwich
metadata.description: Amida, the Buddha of Infinite Light, is one of the most popularly worshipped deities in the Far East. According to sacred scripture, Amida created a paradise, known as the Pure Land (Jo do), where the souls of sentient beings could strive toward enlightenment without the pain and suffering associated with life on earth. In Japan, the worship of Amida became widespread during the Fujiwara period (894-1185), and high ranking aristocrats constructed temple buildings and commissioned paintings that represented Amida's glorious paradise.  The famous sculptor Jo_cho_ created an image of Amida (still remaining at Byo do-in temple in Uji, Japan) of unprecedented elegance and grace. With a round, youthful face, drowsy eyes and shallowly carved drapery, the sculpture conveyed meditative serenity and reassuring calm. The Institute's Amida closely follows Jo_cho_'s prototype. Its surface, now damaged by fire, would have shimmered with a layer of gold. His hands are held in symbolic gestures (mudra): the raised right hand disperses fear and the lowered left hand is open in the gesture of giving or wish granting. 12th Century.     This object is part of Scan The World. Scan the World is a non-profit initiative introduced by MyMiniFactory, through which we are creating a digital archive of fully 3D printable sculptures, artworks and landmarks from across the globe for the public to access for free. Scan the World is an open source, community effort, if you have interesting items around you and would like to contribute, email stw@myminifactory.com to find out how you can help.
